L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference

sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome

oral-bioavailability outcome.

records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: Codeine, a morphinan opioid with an N-methyl group and phenolic substitution, has an absolute oral bioavailability of 80.5% in healthy subjects, supporting high F for the structurally related query morphinan.
Pentazocine, a benzomorphan opioid analgesic, has systemic availability of 0.68–0.70 in cirrhotic patients, above the 20% threshold.
Meptazinol, a phenolic opioid analgesic, has absolute oral bioavailability of 27.9% in cirrhotic patients, above the 20% threshold.
Pethidine/meperidine, an opioid analgesic, has systemic availability of 0.80 in cirrhotic patients, above the 20% threshold.
Naloxegol, a 4,5-epoxymorphinan with the same 14-hydroxy and phenolic scaffold as the query, has a PBPK-predicted oral bioavailability of 0.90.

Several supporting values are from cirrhotic patients, where first-pass metabolism may be reduced; healthy-subject F could be lower.
Naloxegol F is a PBPK simulation rather than a measured clinical value, and its PEG substitution may alter disposition.
The query's 6-keto and 14-hydroxy groups may increase first-pass metabolism relative to codeine or pentazocine, but no card quantifies this.
No solubility, permeability, efflux, or metabolism data specific to the query are supplied.
